name: persuasion_appeals
description: How a text earns belief: ethos moves that build the writer's standing, pathos moves that make a reader feel without cheating them, logos presentation that makes reasoning inspectable, kairos moves that seize the occasion, the propaganda techniques a writer must be able to name in order to describe, resist or satirize them, the commercial copywriting frameworks and their vendor-speak risk, and narrative persuasion — the argument carried by story.

ethos_moves.name: credential placement
ethos_moves.definition: The decision of where in a piece the writer's standing to speak is disclosed — in the first paragraph, at the point of the hardest claim, or in a note at the end.
ethos_moves.example: The claim about ward-level turnout arrives in chapter four, and only there does the writer mention having counted the ballots himself in 1998.
ethos_moves.effect: Standing declared early buys attention; standing declared at the load-bearing claim buys assent for that claim specifically and reads as evidence rather than as advertisement.
ethos_moves.caution: A credential in the opening sentence is spent on readers who have not yet met an argument that needs it.

ethos_moves.name: delayed credential
ethos_moves.definition: Withholding the writer's qualification until the argument has been made on its merits, so that the disclosure confirms rather than compels.
ethos_moves.example: Four pages on what happens to a body in cold water, then: I pulled two of them out myself.
ethos_moves.effect: The reader has already agreed; the credential converts agreement into trust and makes rereading the earlier pages feel different.
ethos_moves.caution: Only works once per piece, and only if the withheld fact would have been the reader's first question.

ethos_moves.name: strategic self-deprecation
ethos_moves.definition: Naming one's own smallness, ignorance or mishap at a chosen point, so that the surrounding claims read as unpuffed.
ethos_moves.example: I had been studying the schedules for a year and still got on the wrong train.
ethos_moves.effect: Lowers the writer's status just enough that the reader stops defending against being lectured.
ethos_moves.register: informal to neutral; rare in institutional prose
ethos_moves.caution: Deprecation about something the reader does not care about is a boast in costume; if the admitted flaw costs nothing, it reads as one.

ethos_moves.name: tribute to the opponent
ethos_moves.definition: Crediting the opposing side with intelligence, motive or a real win before disagreeing with it.
ethos_moves.example: The bill's drafters saw the loophole before anyone else did, and closed it; what they did not see is the second one they opened.
ethos_moves.effect: Removes the reader's suspicion that the writer has not understood what he is attacking, and makes the subsequent disagreement look like judgement rather than reflex.
ethos_moves.caution: Tribute that is immediately cancelled by 'but' in the same sentence reads as procedural, not meant.

ethos_moves.name: borrowed ethos by citation
ethos_moves.definition: Attaching a claim to a source whose standing the reader already accepts, so the source's authority carries the sentence.
ethos_moves.example: The figure is the Bureau's, not mine.
ethos_moves.effect: Transfers credibility from the source to the writer, and moves the reader's scepticism from the claim to the citation.
ethos_moves.caution: The transfer runs both ways: a source the reader distrusts drains standing rather than lending it, and stacking citations for an uncontested point signals anxiety.

ethos_moves.name: insider signaling
ethos_moves.definition: Using a term, a detail or a form of reference the way people inside a field use it, as proof of membership rather than as information.
ethos_moves.example: Calling it the eighty-eight rather than the Flak 36 in a paragraph about gun crews.
ethos_moves.effect: Readers inside the field relax; the writer is not a tourist. Readers outside it register competence even when they miss the reference.
ethos_moves.caution: One signal per stretch of prose; a run of them becomes a wall, and a signal used wrongly destroys more standing than a plain word would ever have built.

ethos_moves.name: disinterest display
ethos_moves.definition: Showing that the writer has nothing to gain from the conclusion — no stake, no client, no side that pays.
ethos_moves.example: I own none of it, and my pension is in the index that would fall if I am right.
ethos_moves.effect: Neutralizes the reader's first defence against persuasion, which is to look for the motive.
ethos_moves.caution: A false or partial disinterest claim is the single most expensive thing in the ethos repertoire to have discovered; state it only where it is verifiable.

ethos_moves.name: interest disclosure
ethos_moves.definition: The inverse move: naming the writer's stake before the reader can find it.
ethos_moves.example: I consulted for one of the two firms in this chapter, in 2019, for a fee I have listed in the notes.
ethos_moves.effect: Converts a discoverable liability into evidence of candour; the reader who was going to find it now finds it from you.
ethos_moves.caution: Disclosure is not absolution — a disclosed conflict still has to be argued past, and burying it in a back note reads as compliance rather than candour.

ethos_moves.name: error admission
ethos_moves.definition: Correcting one's own earlier published claim in the open, with the size of the error stated.
ethos_moves.example: In the first edition I put the figure at nine hundred. It was four hundred and twelve, and the mistake was mine, not the archive's.
ethos_moves.effect: Buys more credibility than the original correctness would have; the reader learns the writer's claims are the kind that get checked.
ethos_moves.caution: Admissions phrased so as to blame the source, the software or the reader's misreading spend the move without buying anything.

ethos_moves.name: the public update
ethos_moves.definition: Reporting that the writer has changed his mind, with the evidence that moved him and the date it landed.
ethos_moves.example: I argued the opposite in 2019. The 2021 replication is what changed it, and I think the earlier piece is now wrong in its second half.
ethos_moves.effect: Demonstrates that the writer's beliefs are attached to evidence rather than to a position, which is the only durable form of authority in a contested field.
ethos_moves.caution: Updating on the trivial while never updating on the load-bearing claim is a performance of open-mindedness and reads as one.

ethos_moves.name: register matching
ethos_moves.definition: Bringing sentence length, vocabulary layer and idiom into the range the audience actually uses, as a claim of shared membership.
ethos_moves.example: A safety briefing for crews written in the crews' own two-clause imperatives rather than in the regulator's noun phrases.
ethos_moves.effect: Removes the friction of translation and signals that the writer has listened to the audience before addressing it.
ethos_moves.register: all; the target register is the variable
ethos_moves.caution: Matching a register the writer does not own produces the tourist effect — the reader hears the imitation, not the membership. Accommodation overdone becomes condescension.

ethos_moves.name: the reluctant conclusion
ethos_moves.definition: Presenting the conclusion as one the writer resisted, arrived at against preference, and would still rather not hold.
ethos_moves.example: I have spent six years arguing that the programme worked. This chapter is the one where I stop.
ethos_moves.effect: Splits the conclusion from the writer's wishes, which is the reader's usual explanation for why a writer believes something.
ethos_moves.caution: Reluctance that is asserted rather than shown is a pose; the reader needs to see the earlier position and what dislodged it.

ethos_moves.name: phronesis display
ethos_moves.definition: Aristotle's first component of ethos: showing practical judgement — that the writer knows how the thing goes in the world, not only what is true about it in principle.
ethos_moves.example: Any plan that requires two agencies to share a database in the first year is not a plan.
ethos_moves.effect: The reader credits the writer with knowing which considerations matter, which is a different and often stronger credential than knowing the facts.
ethos_moves.caution: Practical judgement demonstrated once is authority; asserted repeatedly it becomes the voice of the man who has seen it all, and readers stop believing the specifics.

ethos_moves.name: arete display
ethos_moves.definition: Aristotle's second component: showing character — that the writer holds the values he is asking the reader to act on, at some cost.
ethos_moves.example: The chapter on data hoarding lists the writer's own datasets and the date each was released.
ethos_moves.effect: Aligns the argument's moral demand with the writer's own conduct, closing the gap the reader is already looking for.
ethos_moves.caution: Character shown at no cost is not evidence of character; the display must name something given up.

ethos_moves.name: eunoia display
ethos_moves.definition: Aristotle's third component: showing goodwill toward this audience — that the writer wants their good, not merely the argument's victory.
ethos_moves.example: If you take one thing from this chapter, take the checklist on page 210 and ignore the rest of my quarrel with the standards body.
ethos_moves.effect: Converts the reader from opponent-in-waiting to beneficiary, and licenses harder claims later.
ethos_moves.register: instructional, advocacy, address to a hostile audience
ethos_moves.caution: Goodwill expressed in the abstract is filler; it has to cost the argument something — a concession, a shortcut given away.

ethos_moves.name: unexpected validator
ethos_moves.definition: Citing agreement from a source the reader expects to disagree — a critic of the policy conceding a fact, an industry body confirming a harm.
ethos_moves.example: The estimate is not the campaign's. It is the operator's own filing.
ethos_moves.effect: Defeats the reader's motive-based discount, because the source had every reason to say otherwise.
ethos_moves.caution: Works only when the reader recognizes the source's expected position; an unfamiliar validator is merely another citation.

ethos_moves.name: venue-conferred ethos
ethos_moves.definition: Standing that comes from where the piece appears — the journal, the imprint, the byline's masthead — and the writer's decision whether to lean on it or work as if it were absent.
ethos_moves.example: Writing the same argument for a specialist quarterly and for a Sunday paper, and only in the second case explaining who vets the figures.
ethos_moves.effect: In a venue that already vouches for the writer, credentialing prose is redundant and slightly insulting; outside it, the same prose is necessary.
ethos_moves.caution: Borrowed venue standing collapses when the piece is excerpted, screenshotted or syndicated; write the load-bearing claims to survive the loss of the letterhead.

ethos_moves.name: track-record disclosure
ethos_moves.definition: Publishing the writer's hit rate — past predictions with dates, including the misses — as the credential.
ethos_moves.example: Of the eleven closures I forecast in 2018, seven happened, two were reversed by subsidy, and two were simply wrong.
ethos_moves.effect: Replaces claimed expertise with a measurable one, and pre-empts the reader's search for the failures.
ethos_moves.caution: A record shown only where it is good is card stacking with a graph; the denominator has to be visible.

ethos_moves.name: specificity as credential
ethos_moves.definition: Detail that only someone who was present or who did the work could supply, offered without comment as proof of access.
ethos_moves.example: The room smelled of the machine oil they used on the presses, and the minutes ran to four pages because the chair kept the clock on the table.
ethos_moves.effect: The reader infers the whole body of unstated knowledge behind the detail, which is more persuasive than a statement of qualification.
ethos_moves.caution: Specificity that cannot be checked can also be invented, and readers who catch one fabricated detail retroactively discount every other one.

ethos_moves.name: disclaimed expertise
ethos_moves.definition: Explicitly declining the authority the reader might otherwise assume, and naming what the writer is instead.
ethos_moves.example: I am not an epidemiologist. I am a person who reads their code, and their code does not do what the paper says.
ethos_moves.effect: Narrows the claim to what the writer can actually defend, which makes the narrowed claim harder to dismiss.
ethos_moves.caution: The move goes rotten when the disclaimer is followed by claims that require the disclaimed expertise; then it reads as immunity-seeking.

ethos_moves.name: costly-signal credential
ethos_moves.definition: Standing built on a visible cost the writer paid — years spent, access lost, money forgone, an unpopular position held early.
ethos_moves.example: Nine months of the archive was closed to me after the first article, which is how I know the second one landed.
ethos_moves.effect: The cost is unfakeable in a way that a title is not, and it converts the writer's history into evidence.
ethos_moves.caution: One recitation is a credential; repeated recitation is grievance, and readers reallocate their sympathy quickly.

ethos_moves.name: method disclosure
ethos_moves.definition: Stating how the writer knows — the archives, the interviews, the query, the sample — as an inline part of the claim rather than in an appendix.
ethos_moves.example: This comes from the union's own membership rolls, which I counted twice and which disagree with the federation's published total by nine per cent.
ethos_moves.effect: Lets the reader evaluate the claim's provenance while reading it, which is the difference between being told and being shown.
ethos_moves.caution: Method in every sentence smothers the narrative; disclose at the load-bearing claims and put the rest in the note.

ethos_moves.name: calibrated uncertainty
ethos_moves.definition: Attaching honest, differentiated confidence to claims — sure about this, unsure about that — instead of a uniform tone of certainty or a uniform blanket of hedges.
ethos_moves.example: The date is firm. The motive is my inference. The number of people in the room I do not know and neither does anyone else now living.
ethos_moves.effect: Makes the confident claims worth more, because the reader has seen the writer decline to make one.
ethos_moves.caution: Hedging everything equally is not calibration — it is insurance, and readers read it as evasion.

ethos_moves.name: image repair
ethos_moves.definition: The repertoire for restoring standing after an attack: denial, shifting blame, reducing offensiveness, corrective action, mortification — chosen according to whether the charge is true.
ethos_moves.example: A response that skips denial entirely, states what was done, and gives the date the practice stopped.
ethos_moves.effect: Determines whether the audience's attention returns to the argument or stays on the writer.
ethos_moves.register: public response, preface to a second edition, institutional communication
ethos_moves.caution: Choosing minimization when the charge is true is the standard failure; it converts a survivable error into a credibility problem that outlives the book.

pathos_moves.name: identifiable victim effect
pathos_moves.definition: Naming and particularizing one person so that the reader's sympathy has somewhere to land, in place of an aggregate that has nowhere.
pathos_moves.example: Not four hundred evictions that winter: Mrs Okafor, second floor, who kept the stair light bulb replaced out of her own money for eleven years.
pathos_moves.effect: Readers give — attention, money, belief — to a person and not to a number; the particular case recruits the feeling the aggregate cannot.
pathos_moves.caution: The move is powerful enough to distort: an unrepresentative individual can carry a claim the aggregate would refute. Pair the person with the base rate.

pathos_moves.name: psychic numbing
pathos_moves.definition: The measured collapse of feeling as the number of victims rises — the reader who responds to one responds less to a thousand, and the writer's problem of what to do about it.
pathos_moves.example: Instead of the total, the piece gives one street, then says there were nine hundred such streets.
pathos_moves.effect: Naming the effect in the structure — one first, scale after — recovers some of the response the bare aggregate loses.
pathos_moves.register: reportage on mass harm, history, humanitarian writing
pathos_moves.caution: Knowing the mechanism is also the propagandist's tool: an aggregate can be chosen precisely to deaden a response the particular would provoke.

pathos_moves.name: detail selection as emotional argument
pathos_moves.definition: Choosing which concrete particulars to report, from among many true ones, so that the selection itself does the emotional work no adjective could.
pathos_moves.example: The report lists the recovered items: a house key, a bus pass, a shopping list with four things on it.
pathos_moves.effect: The reader assembles the feeling from the objects and therefore owns it; nothing has been asserted to argue with.
pathos_moves.caution: Selection is an argument, and an argument the reader cannot audit; a set chosen to produce a feeling the full record would not support is dishonest even when every item is true.

pathos_moves.name: second-person immersion
pathos_moves.definition: Putting the reader inside the situation grammatically — you wake, you count the money, you decide — so that the judgement being asked for has to be made from the inside.
pathos_moves.example: You have ninety seconds and two exits, and one of them is where the smoke is coming from.
pathos_moves.effect: Suspends the reader's distance from the choice, which is usually the thing preventing sympathy with the person who made it.
pathos_moves.caution: Sustained past a page it turns coercive, and any detail the reader would not have done breaks the spell and returns them to the third person with a grudge.

pathos_moves.name: restraint as amplifier
pathos_moves.definition: Underwriting the worst moment — plain vocabulary, short clauses, no intensifiers — so the material carries the weight instead of the prose.
pathos_moves.example: They found her on the Tuesday. She had made tea for two.
pathos_moves.effect: The gap between the flatness of the telling and the size of the event is where the reader's feeling forms; the reader supplies what the writer withheld.
pathos_moves.register: all; strongest in reportage and literary nonfiction
pathos_moves.caution: Restraint requires that the facts be sufficient; underwriting a thin event produces nothing but flatness.
aka: the flat register at the terrible moment

pathos_moves.name: the pathetic particular
pathos_moves.definition: A single object made to carry the whole grief — the unworn shoe, the half-finished letter — offered without interpretation.
pathos_moves.example: The kitchen calendar was still on March.
pathos_moves.effect: Concentrates a diffuse emotion into one perceptible thing the reader can hold, which is what makes it recallable a week later.
pathos_moves.caution: One per scene. A catalogue of poignant objects turns the device into a technique the reader can see, and seeing it ends it.

pathos_moves.name: pacing into feeling
pathos_moves.definition: Slowing the sentence and paragraph as the emotional beat approaches — shorter units, more full stops, fewer subordinations — so the reader's reading rate falls with the material.
pathos_moves.example: Three long paragraphs of procedure, then: The door was open. The room was cold. He was still in the chair.
pathos_moves.effect: Reading speed is felt as emotional weight; the deceleration does what an adverb would only have announced.
pathos_moves.caution: Deceleration without a payoff at the bottom reads as portentousness, and the reader who has slowed for nothing speeds up permanently.

pathos_moves.name: dignity preservation
pathos_moves.definition: Writing a suffering person as an agent with a life rather than as an exhibit — their competence, their humour and their refusals kept in the frame with their misfortune.
pathos_moves.example: She had run the depot for nineteen years and she was not going to be photographed crying, so we talked in the office with the door shut.
pathos_moves.effect: Sympathy without condescension; the reader is moved by a person rather than by a condition, and the subject survives the paragraph.
pathos_moves.caution: The failure mode is not cruelty but pity — a subject rendered solely through their worst hour has been used, and readers who know such people can tell.

pathos_moves.name: the ordinary before the rupture
pathos_moves.definition: Establishing the unremarkable texture of a life or a system at length before the break, so the break is measured against something the reader has inhabited.
pathos_moves.example: Eight paragraphs on how the shift handover worked, down to the tea rota, before the paragraph about the night it did not.
pathos_moves.effect: The catastrophe is felt as a loss of a particular ordinariness rather than as an event with a casualty figure.
pathos_moves.caution: The ordinary has to be interesting on its own terms; a reader who is bored during the setup does not become moved at the break.

pathos_moves.name: the enumerated absence
pathos_moves.definition: Counting what is missing rather than what happened — the empty seats, the unclaimed effects, the names read aloud.
pathos_moves.example: The lost-property office kept them for a year: sixty-two coats, nine of them children's.
pathos_moves.effect: Gives the reader a number that stays particular, because each unit of the count is still an object or a person rather than an abstraction.
pathos_moves.caution: Only lands when the count is exact and sourced; a rounded or rhetorical figure turns the device into a gesture.

pathos_moves.name: the posthumous turn
pathos_moves.definition: Writing a person in the present tense of their own life, at length, before disclosing that they did not survive the events described.
pathos_moves.effect: The reader has already invested in a living person, so the disclosure lands as a loss rather than as an item of information.
pathos_moves.example: Two pages on how he taught his daughter to reverse a trailer, and then the date of the inquest.
pathos_moves.caution: The withholding must not read as a trick; if the reader feels manipulated at the reveal, the sympathy converts into resentment of the writer.

pathos_moves.name: the reader as witness
pathos_moves.definition: Positioning the reader as someone who has now seen, and therefore owes attention — not as a participant in the events but as a witness to them.
pathos_moves.example: This is the part nobody filmed, so it has to be written down, and now you are one of the people who know it.
pathos_moves.effect: Converts sympathy into a small obligation, which is the step most emotional writing fails to take.
pathos_moves.caution: Stated too directly it becomes a demand, and readers refuse demands; the obligation is more durable when it is implied by the material.

pathos_moves.name: focused indignation
pathos_moves.definition: Anger given a specific target, a specific act and a specific date, rather than diffused across a condition.
pathos_moves.example: Not 'the system failed her' — the duty officer had the number, had the file open, and went home at six.
pathos_moves.effect: Indignation the reader can act on and check; diffuse outrage produces a mood, focused outrage produces a question.
pathos_moves.caution: A target chosen for its availability rather than its responsibility is scapegoating with better sentences.

pathos_moves.name: the unspoken conclusion
pathos_moves.definition: Laying the facts side by side and stopping one sentence before the inference the reader is now certain to draw.
pathos_moves.example: The safety report was filed in March. The refit was scheduled for November. The fire was in July.
pathos_moves.effect: An inference the reader makes is held more firmly than one they are given, and it cannot be argued with as an assertion because none was made.
pathos_moves.caution: Requires that only one inference is available; if two are, the reader draws the wrong one and the writer has no recourse.
aka: leaving the arithmetic to the reader

pathos_moves.name: sensory anchor
pathos_moves.definition: Fixing an emotional passage to one non-visual sense — a smell, a temperature, a sound — which the reader stores differently from description.
pathos_moves.example: The corridor smelled of wet wool for three days afterwards.
pathos_moves.effect: Recall: the passage returns to the reader later, unbidden, in a way that visual description rarely does.
pathos_moves.caution: Rationed hard. Two sensory anchors in a chapter compete, and neither is the one the reader keeps.

pathos_moves.name: human-scale conversion
pathos_moves.definition: Restating a magnitude in units the body understands — days of a life, distance walked, a room's worth — so the number can be felt as well as read.
pathos_moves.example: Forty minutes of the hearing was spent on it, which is longer than her shift break.
pathos_moves.effect: Moves a quantity out of the abstract register where the reader processes it as information and into one where it registers as cost.
pathos_moves.caution: The conversion must not inflate; a chosen unit that flatters the point is the numerate form of loaded language.

pathos_moves.name: the counter-stereotype detail
pathos_moves.definition: One true particular that breaks the category the reader has already filed the subject under.
pathos_moves.example: The man sleeping in the doorway had a library card in his coat and eleven books out.
pathos_moves.effect: Forces a re-sort: the reader's ready-made feeling about the category no longer fits, and they have to look at the person.
pathos_moves.caution: If the detail is chosen because it is exceptional, the piece has argued that only exceptional members of the category deserve the reader's regard.

pathos_moves.name: consolatio
pathos_moves.definition: The classical consolation: acknowledging the loss at its true size, refusing false comfort, and offering what can honestly be offered — precedent, meaning, or company in the fact.
pathos_moves.example: Nothing here will make this smaller. What follows is only what other people found on the far side of it.
pathos_moves.effect: Earns the reader's trust in a register where most writing is disbelieved, precisely by declining to console prematurely.
pathos_moves.register: elegy, memoir, medical and grief writing
pathos_moves.caution: The genre's failure mode is the silver lining; a consolation that reaches for meaning before the loss is fully stated is heard as dismissal.

pathos_moves.name: the child's-eye rendering
pathos_moves.definition: Reporting an adult catastrophe through what a child noticed and could name, with the adult framing withheld.
pathos_moves.example: The soldiers let him keep the bicycle, and he remembers being pleased about the bicycle.
pathos_moves.effect: The reader supplies the horror the narration does not have available, which is a stronger operation than describing it.
pathos_moves.caution: The device is close to sentimentality's border; the child must be rendered as a person with their own concerns, not as a lens for adult grief.

pathos_moves.name: sympathy budget
pathos_moves.definition: Treating the reader's capacity for feeling as a finite resource across a chapter or a book, and spending it deliberately at chosen points rather than continuously.
pathos_moves.example: One extended scene of the ward per chapter; the rest of the chapter is procurement and law.
pathos_moves.effect: The chosen moments land at full strength because the surrounding prose has not been drawing on the same account.
pathos_moves.caution: Books that are emotionally loud on every page end flat, and their strongest material arrives at a reader who has nothing left to spend on it.

pathos_moves.name: the reader's stake named
pathos_moves.definition: Stating plainly what the matter costs the reader specifically, at the point where the reader's attention would otherwise lapse into charity.
pathos_moves.example: The same clause is in your tenancy agreement, on page four.
pathos_moves.effect: Converts sympathy for others into self-interested attention, which sustains longer and acts sooner.
pathos_moves.caution: Overstating the reader's exposure is the standard fear-appeal failure and is checkable; one exaggeration ends the piece's credibility.

pathos_moves.name: deferred emotion
pathos_moves.definition: Placing the emotional response — the writer's or the subject's — several paragraphs after the event that caused it, where it actually arrived.
pathos_moves.example: He gave the statement, drove home, put the shopping away, and then sat in the car for an hour.
pathos_moves.effect: Matches how feeling behaves in life, so the reader recognizes the sequence rather than watching a performance of grief on cue.
pathos_moves.caution: The deferral must be marked or it reads as omission; the reader needs to feel the delay as delay.

pathos_moves.name: the plain testimony voice
pathos_moves.definition: Quoting a witness at length without cleaning up the syntax, and without a narrating sentence that tells the reader how to hear it.
pathos_moves.example: "I said to him, the door's the wrong way round. That's all I said. The door's the wrong way round."
pathos_moves.effect: Repetition, flatness and the small irrelevance carry the state the speaker was in; a paraphrase would have deleted exactly that.
pathos_moves.caution: Quoting unedited speech can also expose a speaker to ridicule; the writer chooses the extract and owns what the choice does to them.

pathos_moves.name: hope with a next step
pathos_moves.definition: Pairing the emotional peak with one specific, proportionate action, so the feeling has somewhere to discharge.
pathos_moves.example: The consultation closes on the eleventh, and it takes about four minutes.
pathos_moves.effect: Feeling without an outlet decays into helplessness within a page; a named step converts it into intention.
pathos_moves.caution: A step out of proportion to the harm just described insults the reader's feeling — and the house vendor test applies to the ask as much as to the copy.

logos_presentation.name: the visible calculation
logos_presentation.definition: Performing the arithmetic in the prose — the inputs, the operation, the result — instead of presenting only the conclusion.
logos_presentation.example: Eleven sites, four inspectors, a statutory visit every two years: that is sixty-six inspections a year against a capacity of about forty.
logos_presentation.effect: The reader checks the claim as they read it and arrives at the conclusion themselves; a conclusion reached is not the same object as a conclusion received.
logos_presentation.caution: Only for calculations a reader can hold in working memory; anything longer belongs in a table with the result stated in the text.

logos_presentation.name: showing your work
logos_presentation.definition: Exposing the reasoning path — including the wrong turns and the discarded hypothesis — rather than presenting the finished inference.
logos_presentation.example: My first thought was that the rise was seasonal. It is not: the same months in the four preceding years are flat. So it is the tariff or the strike, and the strike ended in April.
logos_presentation.effect: Lets the reader audit the inference and shows which alternatives were considered, which is what distinguishes an argument from an assertion.
logos_presentation.caution: The performance of showing work while omitting the one alternative that survives is worse than not showing it at all, because it borrows the credibility of transparency.

logos_presentation.name: the falsifiable commitment
logos_presentation.definition: Stating in advance what observation would make the writer abandon the claim, and by when it could be observed.
logos_presentation.example: If the 2027 census shows the ward under nine thousand, this chapter's argument is wrong and I will say so.
logos_presentation.effect: Converts a position into a prediction, which readers score differently and which the writer can no longer quietly retreat from.
logos_presentation.caution: A falsifier chosen because it will never be measured is unfalsifiability wearing the costume of rigour.

logos_presentation.name: steelman by quotation
logos_presentation.definition: Putting the opposing case in the opponent's own published words, at their strongest, before answering — rather than in the writer's reconstruction of them.
logos_presentation.example: Here is the objection as its author states it, in full, from the 2020 paper; the paragraph after this one is my answer.
logos_presentation.effect: Removes the reader's suspicion of a rigged summary, which is the suspicion that neutralizes most refutations.
logos_presentation.caution: Quote long enough to include the load-bearing clause; a fair-looking short quotation that drops the qualifier is contextomy with better manners.

logos_presentation.name: the concession budget
logos_presentation.definition: Deciding in advance how much of the opposing case to grant, and spending it on the points where granting costs the argument least and buys the most credibility.
logos_presentation.example: Grant the cost overrun and the delay; contest only the claim that the design was unbuildable.
logos_presentation.effect: A concession made early and specifically inoculates against the reader's own objection arriving later with more force.
logos_presentation.caution: Two failure modes: conceding nothing, which reads as advocacy, and conceding the crux, which ends the argument while the prose continues.

logos_presentation.name: argument mapping in prose
logos_presentation.definition: Making the support structure explicit in the sentences — this claim rests on these two, of which the second is the weaker — so the reader can see the shape without a diagram.
logos_presentation.example: Everything below depends on the shipping figures being complete. If they are not, the second half of this chapter fails and the first half stands.
logos_presentation.effect: Tells the reader where to push, which paradoxically strengthens the argument by directing scrutiny to the place the writer has already reinforced.
logos_presentation.caution: Prose that maps itself constantly reads like a specification; map at the chapter's hinges and let the rest carry itself.

logos_presentation.name: burden acknowledgment
logos_presentation.definition: Naming which side has to prove what, and accepting the burden the writer's own claim carries rather than letting it drift to the reader.
logos_presentation.example: I am the one claiming a change in policy caused this, so the counterfactual is mine to establish, and here is the attempt.
logos_presentation.effect: Pre-empts the commonest structural objection and signals that the writer knows what would count as proof.
logos_presentation.caution: Acknowledging the burden and then not discharging it is worse than never raising it — the reader is now watching for exactly what is missing.

logos_presentation.name: the numbered argument
logos_presentation.definition: Setting out the case as enumerated propositions, so each can be attacked or granted separately.
logos_presentation.example: The case has three parts. One: the shortfall is real. Two: it is not demographic. Three: the remedy on the table addresses the demographic version.
logos_presentation.effect: Prevents the whole argument from being dismissed on one weak limb, and gives an opponent a specific thing to answer.
logos_presentation.register: policy memo, legal brief, analytical essay
logos_presentation.caution: Numbering invites the reader to count; a list whose items overlap or whose third item is filler advertises the padding.

logos_presentation.name: definitional groundwork
logos_presentation.definition: Fixing the sense of the argument's contested terms before the argument uses them, and saying which senses are being set aside.
logos_presentation.example: By 'shortage' I mean unfilled posts at the advertised rate. I am not using it to mean an insufficiency of trained people, and the two figures differ by a factor of six.
logos_presentation.effect: Removes the equivocation route by which most disagreements in this area are conducted, and lets the reader hold the writer to one meaning.
logos_presentation.caution: A definition chosen because it delivers the conclusion is a persuasive definition; state the cost of the choice as well as the choice.

logos_presentation.name: the crux named
logos_presentation.definition: Identifying the single proposition on which the disagreement actually turns, and saying that the rest of the dispute is downstream of it.
logos_presentation.example: We agree on every number in this table. The disagreement is entirely about whether the 2016 reclassification is comparable, and that is the only question worth the next ten pages.
logos_presentation.effect: Collapses a sprawling dispute into a tractable one and prevents the reader from mistaking peripheral agreement for progress.
logos_presentation.caution: Naming a crux that suits the writer's strengths rather than the actual dependency is a frame grab; the opponent's stated crux must at least be addressed.

logos_presentation.name: order-of-magnitude check
logos_presentation.definition: Testing a claim's plausibility by rough estimation in the open, before treating any precise figure as meaningful.
logos_presentation.example: Two million journeys a day would mean every adult in the city travelling twice; the figure is either wrong or counting something else.
logos_presentation.effect: Shows the reader a cheap, repeatable test they can apply to the next figure they meet, and disposes of bad numbers without a source fight.
logos_presentation.caution: The estimate has to be stated as an estimate; a rough figure that acquires decimal places two paragraphs later is spurious precision.

logos_presentation.name: disconfirming evidence first
logos_presentation.definition: Leading with the strongest data against the writer's own position, then arguing past it.
logos_presentation.example: The best evidence against everything that follows is the Rotterdam trial, which found no effect at all. Here is why I think it does not settle the question.
logos_presentation.effect: The reader who was holding that objection in reserve has it defused at the start, and reads the rest without the counter-argument running underneath.
logos_presentation.caution: Requires that the answer actually be good; leading with the strongest objection and answering it weakly hands the reader the case against.

logos_presentation.name: the confidence label
logos_presentation.definition: Attaching an explicit likelihood or evidential grade to a claim — near-certain, likely, an even bet — rather than letting the prose imply uniform certainty.
logos_presentation.example: Near-certain: the meeting happened. Likely: it was about the contract. A guess: it is why the tender was reissued.
logos_presentation.effect: Lets the reader carry forward a differentiated picture, and lets the writer make a speculative claim without smuggling it in at the same weight as a documented one.
logos_presentation.caution: Labels used as decoration — everything 'likely' — destroy the scale they depend on.

logos_presentation.name: the counterfactual stated
logos_presentation.definition: Making explicit what the writer thinks would have happened absent the cause being argued for, so the causal claim has a comparison to be judged against.
logos_presentation.example: Without the subsidy the plant would have closed in 2011, on the same schedule as the other two of its generation.
logos_presentation.effect: Converts a bare causal assertion into a claim with a testable alternative, which is the only form in which readers can weigh it.
logos_presentation.caution: An unstated counterfactual is where most causal writing hides its weakest assumption; a stated one that is merely asserted has only moved the problem.

logos_presentation.name: the mechanism supplied
logos_presentation.definition: Giving the physical, institutional or economic pathway by which the alleged cause produces the alleged effect, step by step.
logos_presentation.example: The tariff raises the input price, the mill's contracts are annual, so the effect appears in the following January's accounts and not before.
logos_presentation.effect: A correlation with a mechanism is a different evidential object from a correlation without one, and readers weight it accordingly.
logos_presentation.caution: A plausible mechanism is not evidence that this mechanism operated; state which steps are documented and which are inferred.

logos_presentation.name: rival explanation eliminated
logos_presentation.definition: Listing the competing explanations for the same evidence and ruling each out on stated grounds before advancing the writer's own.
logos_presentation.example: It is not seasonality, not the reclassification, and not the strike; each fails on the timing, and here are the three dates.
logos_presentation.effect: Turns an assertion of the best explanation into a demonstration of it, which is what inference to the best explanation actually requires.
logos_presentation.caution: A rival list that omits the strongest rival is the most common failure; readers who know the field will supply it, and everything else collapses.

logos_presentation.name: the assumption ledger
logos_presentation.definition: Collecting the argument's load-bearing assumptions in one place, each with what it would take to break it.
logos_presentation.example: Three assumptions: that the registry is complete after 1994, that the categories did not change, and that the deaths are recorded in the district of occurrence.
logos_presentation.effect: Lets a later reader — or the writer at revision — see exactly which brick to test, and makes an honest argument auditable.
logos_presentation.caution: A ledger that lists only the safe assumptions is worse than none: it certifies rigour while omitting the exposure.

logos_presentation.name: the scope statement
logos_presentation.definition: Saying what the argument does not claim, and about which cases, populations or periods it is silent.
logos_presentation.example: This is an argument about metropolitan authorities between 1998 and 2015. It says nothing about the counties and nothing after the reorganisation.
logos_presentation.effect: Prevents the reader from testing the claim against a case it never covered, which is how most arguments are wrongly refuted.
logos_presentation.caution: Scope narrowed after an objection is retreat; scope stated up front is discipline. Readers can tell which one they are watching.

logos_presentation.name: the limiting case check
logos_presentation.definition: Running the argument to its boundary — zero, one, everybody, forever — in the open, to show that it does not break there.
logos_presentation.example: If the rule applied to a single household the cost would be nine pounds; if it applied to every household in the country it would be four hundred million. Both are affordable, which is the point.
logos_presentation.effect: Demonstrates robustness cheaply, and forestalls the reductio the reader was assembling.
logos_presentation.caution: Only run the check where the argument survives it; an unacknowledged boundary failure noticed by the reader ends the piece.

logos_presentation.name: the audit trail
logos_presentation.definition: Publishing the underlying material — dataset, query, document set, interview list — so the claim is reproducible rather than merely sourced.
logos_presentation.example: The three queries are in the appendix; the extract is on the publisher's site with the date of download.
logos_presentation.effect: Shifts the claim from testimony to demonstration, and makes the writer's future errors findable, which is itself a credibility position.
logos_presentation.caution: An audit trail that cannot actually be run — dead links, a dataset behind a licence — is worse than an honest note saying the material is restricted.

logos_presentation.name: worked example before the rule
logos_presentation.definition: Running one full case through the reasoning in concrete terms, then stating the general principle it instantiates.
logos_presentation.example: Follow one invoice from the depot to the audit; the principle at the end of it is that nobody in the chain can see both prices.
logos_presentation.effect: The reader arrives at the abstraction holding a case that fits it, which is the difference between understanding a rule and being able to apply one.
logos_presentation.register: instructional writing, popular science, technical explanation
logos_presentation.caution: The example must be typical; a case chosen for vividness that the rule then over-generalizes teaches the wrong rule.

kairos_and_timing.name: the teachable moment
kairos_and_timing.definition: Publishing an explanation at the point where an event has just made an audience want it, rather than when the writer finished thinking about it.
kairos_and_timing.example: The piece explaining how deposit insurance works, filed the morning after the queue outside the branch.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Attention that no amount of craft could have manufactured is already present; the writing only has to be worth it.
kairos_and_timing.caution: The window is short and the explanation is often needed before the facts are stable; write what is structural and date what is not.

kairos_and_timing.name: news-peg timing
kairos_and_timing.definition: Attaching a piece with a long shelf life to a current event that makes it publishable now.
kairos_and_timing.example: A decade of research on ferry safety, run in the week of a report's release.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Supplies editors and readers with the answer to 'why now', which is the question that kills most otherwise good pieces.
kairos_and_timing.caution: A peg that bears no real relation to the argument reads as opportunism, and the piece dies with the news cycle it borrowed.

kairos_and_timing.name: anniversary framing
kairos_and_timing.definition: Using a round-numbered interval since an event as the occasion for reassessment.
kairos_and_timing.example: Twenty years on, the inquiry's four recommendations are worth checking one at a time.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Creates an occasion where none existed, and licenses retrospective judgement that would look arbitrary on an ordinary Tuesday.
kairos_and_timing.caution: The reassessment has to be real; an anniversary piece with nothing new is the most predictable filler in nonfiction, and readers recognize the shape immediately.

kairos_and_timing.name: the cold take
kairos_and_timing.definition: Deliberately publishing after the argument has cooled, when the facts are settled and the audience's positions are no longer defended in public.
kairos_and_timing.example: The account that waits for the litigation to end and the participants to be willing to talk.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Buys accuracy, access and a reader who is no longer in a fight — and is often the only condition under which a mind changes.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Cold has a floor: past a certain distance the audience that cared has dispersed, and the piece needs a new reason to exist.

kairos_and_timing.name: prebuttal
kairos_and_timing.definition: Publishing the answer to an argument before that argument is made, so the audience meets the objection already inoculated.
kairos_and_timing.example: Two days before the report lands, a piece explaining what its methodology can and cannot show.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Sets the terms on which the later material is read, and denies it the advantage of arriving first.
kairos_and_timing.register: policy communication, campaign writing, scientific commentary
kairos_and_timing.caution: Prebuttal of an argument nobody was going to make manufactures the opponent it answers, and gives that opponent free standing.

kairos_and_timing.name: seasonal opening
kairos_and_timing.definition: Beginning from the calendar — the term starting, the accounts closing, the light going — as the occasion that makes the subject present.
kairos_and_timing.example: Every September the same four hundred families make the same appeal, and every September it is refused for the same reason.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Grounds an abstract recurring problem in a moment the reader is currently living in.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Seasonal openings are the most imitated in the form; the season has to be doing structural work rather than supplying weather.

kairos_and_timing.name: exigence claiming
kairos_and_timing.definition: Asserting that the moment demands this argument — that a decision is imminent, a window closing, a harm ongoing — as an explicit part of the case.
kairos_and_timing.example: The consultation closes in eleven days, after which the classification is fixed for a decade.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Converts a topic into an occasion and gives the reader a reason to read now rather than later, which is usually never.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Manufactured urgency is the commonest abuse in the category and is checkable; one invented deadline discredits the argument it was meant to carry.

kairos_and_timing.name: focusing event
kairos_and_timing.definition: A sudden, visible, harmful event that concentrates public and official attention on a problem specialists have been describing for years, and the writer's decision to use it as the entry point.
kairos_and_timing.example: The bridge collapse gives eight hundred pages of maintenance backlog a reader.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Long-standing structural argument becomes publishable and legible; the event supplies the attention the argument could not.
kairos_and_timing.caution: The event is not the argument, and a piece that leans on it inherits its shelf life; make the structural case survive the reader's forgetting the event.

kairos_and_timing.name: the second-day angle
kairos_and_timing.definition: Deliberately ceding the first report of an event and publishing the question it raises — why it happened, who decided, what is now different.
kairos_and_timing.example: Everyone has the fire. The second-day piece has the inspection regime that exempted the building.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Trades the perishable advantage of being first for the durable one of being the piece that is cited afterwards.
kairos_and_timing.caution: The angle has to be reported rather than opined; second-day commentary without new material is the form's characteristic waste.

kairos_and_timing.name: embargo timing
kairos_and_timing.definition: Writing to a release time set by someone else — a report, an earnings statement, a court's judgement — so that the analysis appears with the material rather than after it.
kairos_and_timing.example: The piece is written from the embargoed copy on Tuesday and publishes at seven on Wednesday with the finding.
kairos_and_timing.effect: The reader meets the primary material and its interpretation together, which is the only moment at which interpretation reliably travels with it.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Analysis written before the reaction can be seen has to be robust to the reaction; embargo pieces age badly when the interesting thing turns out to be the response.

kairos_and_timing.name: evergreen framing
kairos_and_timing.definition: Writing so that the piece has no perishable references at all — no 'last week', no current officeholder — so it can be read at any point.
kairos_and_timing.example: A chapter on how planning objections work that never names the current minister or the current fee.
kairos_and_timing.effect: The piece keeps its usefulness and its citations for years, at the price of the attention a peg would have supplied.
kairos_and_timing.register: book-length nonfiction, reference and guide writing
kairos_and_timing.caution: Evergreen prose drifts toward the airless; anchor it in specific cases with dates rather than in timeless generality.

kairos_and_timing.name: ripeness claim
kairos_and_timing.definition: Arguing that the conditions for a change now exist — the evidence has accumulated, the objection has been answered, the cost has fallen — so that delay no longer has a defence.
kairos_and_timing.example: The three reasons given for waiting in 2009 have each since been met; there is no fourth.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Shifts the argument from whether to when, which is a much weaker ground for an opponent to hold.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Ripeness asserted without disposing of the actual current objection reads as impatience and invites the counsel of delay in reply.

kairos_and_timing.name: the counsel of delay
kairos_and_timing.definition: The reply that the cause is just but the moment is wrong — more consultation, a better vehicle, the next parliament — used to defer indefinitely without ever contesting the merits.
kairos_and_timing.example: Nobody disputes the finding. The recommendation is that it be revisited after the review, which reports in two years.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Converts a substantive defeat into a procedural one and moves the burden onto the person asking for the change to ask again later.
kairos_and_timing.caution: As a writer's move it is close to indefensible; as an object of analysis it is essential — name the pattern, count the deferrals, and give the dates.
aka: the appeal to a more convenient season

kairos_and_timing.name: the hot take
kairos_and_timing.definition: Publishing a strong position on an event before the facts that would determine it are available, timed to the peak of attention.
kairos_and_timing.example: The verdict on the cause, filed while the building is still burning.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Maximum reach, minimum durability; the take is read by many and cited by nobody, and it is what the writer is remembered for if it is wrong.
kairos_and_timing.caution: The genre's cost is cumulative and invisible: each take spends a little standing, and the account only comes due when a slow piece needs to be believed.

kairos_and_timing.name: the friday news dump
kairos_and_timing.definition: Releasing damaging material at the moment of least attention — end of week, eve of a holiday, under a larger story — so that it is technically public and practically unread.
kairos_and_timing.example: The revised figures appear at half past five on the Friday before a bank holiday.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Satisfies the letter of disclosure while defeating its purpose; the timing is the message.
kairos_and_timing.register: institutional communication; for writers, an object of analysis
kairos_and_timing.caution: Detectable and reportable: timestamp the release, note the surrounding news, and the pattern becomes the story.

kairos_and_timing.name: pre-crisis framing
kairos_and_timing.definition: Establishing the terms, the numbers and the responsibilities before the event that will make them contested, so that the later argument is conducted on prepared ground.
kairos_and_timing.example: A piece on flood-defence responsibility written in the dry summer, cited by everyone in November.
kairos_and_timing.effect: In the crisis nobody is persuadable and nothing can be established; work done beforehand is the only work that is available then.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Pre-crisis pieces have no audience by definition; write them for the archive and expect the readership to arrive late.

kairos_and_timing.name: the deadline peg
kairos_and_timing.definition: Timing to a scheduled decision point in someone else's calendar — a vote, a licence expiry, a statutory deadline — rather than to an event.
kairos_and_timing.example: The licence lapses on the thirty-first, and the successor regime has not been laid before the house.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Gives the piece a built-in clock and a specific set of readers who must act before it runs out.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Deadlines slip, and a piece that stakes everything on one becomes an artefact of a date that did not matter; make the underlying argument free-standing.

kairos_and_timing.name: the report-release peg
kairos_and_timing.definition: Timing to the publication of a document — an audit, a statistical release, a court judgement — whose contents the writer has already worked through.
kairos_and_timing.example: Six weeks with the draft methodology, so that on the morning the numbers land the piece is about what they mean.
kairos_and_timing.effect: Converts an event everyone covers into one only the prepared writer can interpret; preparation is the whole of the advantage.
kairos_and_timing.caution: Preparing an interpretation before seeing the result is where analysts pre-commit to the wrong story; write the frame, not the conclusion.

propaganda_techniques.name: bandwagon
propaganda_techniques.definition: The Institute for Propaganda Analysis device of urging an audience to adopt a position because everyone in the group already has, with belonging rather than truth as the offered reason.
propaganda_techniques.example: Families across the county have already signed. Add your name to theirs.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Substitutes the fear of standing outside the group for any assessment of the claim; the reader's question shifts from 'is it so' to 'am I with them'.
cues: "join the millions"
"the whole country now agrees"
counts of adherents where the claim is about fact
second-person plural pressing toward a group boundary
propaganda_techniques.register: campaign material, advertising; for writers, an object to describe or mimic
propaganda_techniques.caution: Writers describing a movement can reproduce the device unintentionally by reporting adoption figures as if they were evidence.

propaganda_techniques.name: card stacking
propaganda_techniques.definition: The IPA device of presenting only the evidence favouring one side while omitting, minimizing or burying the rest, so that a true-seeming account is systematically one-sided.
propaganda_techniques.example: A safety record described entirely through the years since the last incident.
propaganda_techniques.effect: The audience reasons correctly from a rigged sample and reaches the intended conclusion without being lied to in any single sentence.
cues: comparisons that begin at a chosen year
no adverse case mentioned anywhere
sources all from one side of the dispute
figures given as totals where rates would be unfavourable
propaganda_techniques.register: corporate and government communication; satirists reproduce it by making the omission conspicuous
propaganda_techniques.caution: The hardest device to detect from inside a text — it is defined by what is absent, so detection means checking against the full record.

propaganda_techniques.name: glittering generality
propaganda_techniques.definition: The IPA device of attaching a virtue word with warm associations and no fixed content — freedom, resilience, common sense — to a specific proposal, so the proposal inherits the warmth without argument.
propaganda_techniques.example: A resilient, community-first approach to service redesign.
propaganda_techniques.effect: The audience assents to the value and finds itself having assented to the policy; the word's vagueness is what makes the transfer possible.
cues: abstract virtue nouns doing the work of specifics
no operational definition anywhere in the text
the word would be unopposable if stated alone
adjective stacks with no measurable referent
propaganda_techniques.register: political and institutional prose; a staple of mock-institutional satire
propaganda_techniques.caution: Almost invisible in one's own draft, because the writer knows what the word means to them; the test is whether an opponent could use it for the opposite policy.

propaganda_techniques.name: name calling
propaganda_techniques.definition: The IPA device of attaching a bad-associated label to a person, group or proposal, so that the label does the work of an argument against it.
propaganda_techniques.example: The scheme is described throughout as a levy, never as a charge, and its supporters as the levy lobby.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Predisposes the audience to reject without examining, and makes any later neutral discussion feel like a defence.
cues: a consistent pejorative substituted for the neutral term
labels applied to persons where the dispute is about claims
suffixes and epithets doing evaluative work (-ist, -crat, so-called)
propaganda_techniques.register: polemic, campaign material; satire reproduces it by overloading the label
propaganda_techniques.caution: The logical defect — treating the source's character as evidence about the claim — belongs to the fallacies file; here the interest is in the labelling machinery itself.

propaganda_techniques.name: plain folks
propaganda_techniques.definition: The IPA device by which a powerful speaker presents themselves as ordinary — the kitchen table, the local idiom, the modest car — so that their interests read as the audience's own.
propaganda_techniques.example: The chairman's letter to shareholders opens with the price of a pint in his home town.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Suppresses the audience's attention to the speaker's actual position and interests, which is the information most relevant to evaluating what they say.
cues: deliberate register-lowering by a speaker who elsewhere writes formally
domestic props in political or corporate settings
"like you and me" from someone unlike the reader in the relevant respect
propaganda_techniques.caution: Distinguish from honest register matching, which does not conceal the speaker's position; the device is defined by the concealment, not the plain language.

propaganda_techniques.name: testimonial
propaganda_techniques.definition: The IPA device of having a respected or liked figure endorse a claim or product, so that regard for the person transfers to the thing endorsed.
propaganda_techniques.example: A retired inspector's endorsement on the cover of a safety-equipment brochure.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Where the endorser has relevant expertise and no undisclosed interest, the endorsement is legitimate evidence; where either fails, it is pure transfer.
cues: endorsement by fame rather than by relevant expertise
no disclosure of payment or relationship
the endorser's expertise is in a different domain from the claim
quotation marks around praise with no verifiable specifics
propaganda_techniques.caution: The neutral case is narrow: relevant expertise, disclosed interest, and a claim the endorser is in a position to have checked. Everything else is the fault version.

propaganda_techniques.name: transfer
propaganda_techniques.definition: The IPA device of placing a proposal next to a revered symbol — flag, cross, laboratory coat, uniform — so that the symbol's authority flows to the proposal without a stated connection.
propaganda_techniques.example: The product's advertising is shot entirely in what looks like a hospital.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Borrows sanctity or authority the sponsor has not earned, and does it below the level at which an audience formulates objections.
cues: institutional imagery or vocabulary unconnected to the claim
borrowed technical register (clinically, engineered, certified) without a certificate
adjacency to a revered name with no stated relation
propaganda_techniques.caution: In prose the device is carried by diction rather than pictures: the vocabulary of one respected domain applied to an unrelated one.

propaganda_techniques.name: atrocity framing
propaganda_techniques.definition: The selection and foregrounding of the enemy's worst attributed acts — often uncorroborated, often against children — as the frame through which every other question about a conflict is presented.
propaganda_techniques.example: Every discussion of the trade dispute opens with the same unverified account of what happened at the border post.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Forecloses proportionality and negotiation, because a party defined by atrocity cannot be treated as one with interests.
cues: unattributed accounts of extreme cruelty repeated without new sourcing
atrocity narrative preceding every unrelated policy question
emotional detail rich, provenance thin
no corresponding accounting of one's own side
propaganda_techniques.register: wartime and conflict communication; historians and reporters must name it to write about it
propaganda_techniques.caution: Atrocities also happen. The device is not the reporting of atrocity but its use as a universal frame and its exemption from the sourcing standards applied elsewhere.

propaganda_techniques.name: euphemism treadmill exploitation
propaganda_techniques.definition: Deliberately keeping a policy's vocabulary one step ahead of public understanding, replacing each term as it acquires the connotation the practice actually has.
propaganda_techniques.example: Redundancies become restructuring, then rightsizing, then a talent realignment, with the practice unchanged throughout.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Resets the audience's accumulated moral knowledge about the practice every few years, and makes historical comparison difficult by breaking the search term.
cues: a new institutional term for an old practice with no change in the practice
the term is unusable outside the institution
official documents and affected people use different words for the same event
the previous term now sounds frank
propaganda_techniques.register: institutional prose; the richest single vein for mock-institutional satire
propaganda_techniques.caution: Writers describing the practice should give the plain word once and then quote the official term, rather than adopting it for readability.

propaganda_techniques.name: firehose of falsehood
propaganda_techniques.definition: As a propaganda programme rather than a debating tactic: high-volume, multichannel, continuous and openly inconsistent messaging that aims at exhaustion and generalized disbelief rather than at any particular belief.
propaganda_techniques.example: Six official accounts of the same incident in nine days, across four outlets, none withdrawn when the next appears.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Defeats verification by economics — refutation costs more than assertion — and leaves an audience that believes nothing, which is the operational goal.
cues: mutually contradictory official accounts left standing
no retraction after refutation
volume and speed prioritized over consistency
the same claim seeded through unrelated-looking channels
propaganda_techniques.register: state and organized communication; the fallacies file owns its use as an individual debate stratagem
propaganda_techniques.caution: Refuting each claim serves the programme by consuming the refuter; naming the pattern and the pattern's purpose is the response that scales.

propaganda_techniques.name: manufactured consensus
propaganda_techniques.definition: Constructing the appearance of broad agreement — coordinated statements, multiplied outlets, a chorus of signatories with one funder — to make a contested position look settled.
propaganda_techniques.example: Eleven identically argued op-eds in regional papers over a fortnight, each by a different local figure.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Recruits the audience's reasonable heuristic that widely held expert positions are usually right, and turns it against them.
cues: identical framing and phrasing across nominally independent voices
signatory lists with a shared funder or address
"experts agree" with no named experts
publication clustered in a narrow window
propaganda_techniques.caution: Detection is a sourcing exercise, not a reading one: trace funding and authorship rather than arguing with the content.

propaganda_techniques.name: astroturfing
propaganda_techniques.definition: Manufacturing the appearance of spontaneous grassroots support, with the sponsor's role concealed behind invented local groups, template letters and paid participants.
propaganda_techniques.example: Two hundred letters to the council, in nine variants of one paragraph, from addresses in a district with no branch of the organization.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Converts sponsor money into the political currency of apparent public feeling, which decision-makers are obliged to weigh.
cues: near-identical letters or comments with shuffled synonyms
groups with no history before the campaign
no accessible membership, accounts or address
local voices using the sponsor's technical vocabulary
propaganda_techniques.register: public affairs, regulatory comment, online campaigning
propaganda_techniques.caution: For satirists the genre is a gift, because template prose read aloud in sequence indicts itself; for reporters the evidence is in the metadata, not the text.

propaganda_techniques.name: illusory truth exploitation
propaganda_techniques.definition: Exploiting the measured tendency of repeated statements to be rated truer with each exposure, by repeating a claim across time and channels regardless of refutation.
propaganda_techniques.example: The same seven-word phrase in every release for two years, unchanged after the correction.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Familiarity is misread by the audience as prior verification; the claim feels checked because it feels known.
cues: verbatim repetition of a fixed formula across contexts
claim persists unchanged after correction
phrasing optimized for repeatability rather than precision
the audience can quote it but cannot source it
propaganda_techniques.caution: Corrections that restate the false claim in order to deny it feed the same mechanism; state the true version first and lead with it.

propaganda_techniques.name: us-them totalization
propaganda_techniques.definition: Rendering a population as a single agent with a single will, so that every member carries the attributed acts of any member and no internal distinction survives.
propaganda_techniques.example: A whole profession referred to throughout in the singular, as one entity with one motive.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Removes the individual case from consideration in advance, which is the precondition for collective punishment and for the reader's indifference to it.
cues: a group named in the singular as an actor
"they" with no antecedent narrower than a nationality or a profession
attributed motives held uniformly by millions
no dissenting member ever quoted
propaganda_techniques.caution: The move is easy to reproduce accidentally in any writing about institutions; the test is whether a named individual could be substituted for the collective noun.

propaganda_techniques.name: dehumanizing metaphor
propaganda_techniques.definition: Describing a group consistently through a source domain reserved for non-persons — vermin, contagion, flood, infestation — until the metaphor's entailments govern what may be proposed.
propaganda_techniques.example: A decade of official documents in which arrivals are measured in the vocabulary of hydrology.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Metaphor supplies the policy: things that flood are dammed, things that infest are eradicated, and the argument is never made explicitly enough to be refuted.
cues: one source domain used exclusively for one group
quantity language used for people (waves, surges, influx)
verbs of pest control or sanitation applied to persons
the metaphor's entailments appearing as policy proposals
propaganda_techniques.register: conflict and migration rhetoric; historically the reliable precursor to violence
propaganda_techniques.caution: Writers reporting such rhetoric should quote it rather than adopt its vocabulary in their own narration, which is how it spreads into neutral prose.

propaganda_techniques.name: scapegoating
propaganda_techniques.definition: Assigning a complex, diffusely caused harm to a single identifiable group whose punishment is presented as the remedy.
propaganda_techniques.example: The town's twenty-year industrial decline explained in a leaflet by the arrival of eleven families in 2019.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Provides an explanation with an action attached, which is more satisfying than an accurate account with none, and directs grievance away from the actual causes.
cues: a small or powerless group credited with system-scale effects
the proposed remedy is punitive rather than structural
timelines that do not fit the attributed cause
the group named before the mechanism is stated
propaganda_techniques.caution: The counter is arithmetic and chronology rather than moral objection; show the size of the attributed cause against the size of the effect.

propaganda_techniques.name: the big lie
propaganda_techniques.definition: A falsehood on a scale that defeats ordinary scepticism, on the reasoning that audiences will assume nobody would fabricate something so large, and that its very scale makes partial denial impossible.
propaganda_techniques.example: A total reversal of who initiated a documented sequence of events, asserted without qualification and repeated as settled background.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Forces opponents into the position of denying an entire account rather than correcting a detail, which is slower, duller and less quotable.
cues: a claim so large that refuting it requires re-narrating everything
asserted as background rather than argued
no falsifiable specifics offered
supporters treat requests for evidence as bad faith
propaganda_techniques.caution: Refutation by detail loses; the effective counter is a competing complete account with dates and documents.

propaganda_techniques.name: flag-waving
propaganda_techniques.definition: Presenting a contested proposal as an expression of national or group loyalty, so that opposing the proposal reads as disloyalty to the group.
propaganda_techniques.example: A procurement decision defended entirely in the vocabulary of national pride, with no reference to the tender.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Converts a policy question into an identity test, on which most audiences do not deliberate at all.
cues: national vocabulary in a technical dispute
opponents described as against the country rather than against the policy
the merits never argued in the same document
collective possessives (our, the nation's) attached to a private interest
propaganda_techniques.register: political communication, defence and trade rhetoric
propaganda_techniques.caution: Distinguish from a genuine argument about national interest, which states an interest and can be contested on it.

propaganda_techniques.name: white propaganda
propaganda_techniques.definition: Openly attributed persuasion: the source is correctly identified and the material is accurate, but selection and emphasis serve the sponsor's ends.
propaganda_techniques.example: A ministry's public-information campaign, correctly badged, presenting only the statistics that favour the programme.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Retains credibility because it can be checked, and works through emphasis rather than falsehood — which makes it the most durable of the three attribution classes.
cues: correct attribution and accurate facts
systematic one-sidedness in selection
no adverse data in a document that would have it
publication timed to a decision
propaganda_techniques.caution: Neutral only in the sense that open advocacy is legitimate; the card-stacking inside it is not, and the honest badge often licenses it.

propaganda_techniques.name: gray propaganda
propaganda_techniques.definition: Material whose source is deliberately left unclear — no false attribution, but no true one either — so that audiences supply a more credible origin than the actual sponsor.
propaganda_techniques.example: A well-produced report with no named authorship, circulating with the appearance of an independent institute's work.
propaganda_techniques.effect: The audience's own inference does the laundering; nothing false has been asserted about the source because nothing has been asserted at all.
cues: no author, funder or address in a document that would normally carry them
institutional design language without an institution
circulation through intermediaries who do not know the origin
declining to answer sourcing questions
propaganda_techniques.caution: The absence of attribution is itself the finding; report the gap rather than speculating about the sponsor.

propaganda_techniques.name: black propaganda
propaganda_techniques.definition: Material falsely attributed to another party — forged documents, impersonated outlets, statements planted in an opponent's voice.
propaganda_techniques.example: A circular purporting to come from a union executive, announcing a position the executive never took.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Damages the impersonated party twice: by the content, and by the doubt it casts on their genuine communications afterwards.
cues: an outlet or letterhead close to but not identical with a real one
no copy in the purported source's own archive
a position slightly more extreme than the party's known record
first circulation through channels hostile to the purported author
propaganda_techniques.caution: Writers must never produce specimens that could circulate as genuine; describe the technique, quote from the documented historical case, and do not manufacture an example.

propaganda_techniques.name: information laundering
propaganda_techniques.definition: Moving a claim through a chain of citations — a blog cited by an aggregator, cited by a trade outlet, cited by a broadsheet — until the last link can be cited as though it were independently established.
propaganda_techniques.example: A figure invented in a press release is quoted by three outlets and returns to the sponsor's next release cited to the third.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Manufactures the appearance of corroboration out of a single unsourced origin, and makes the origin practically unfindable.
cues: every source ultimately citing the same one
the figure identical across outlets to an implausible precision
citation chains that loop back to the sponsor
no primary document anywhere in the chain
propaganda_techniques.caution: The check is mechanical: follow every citation to a primary document or a dead end, and report the dead end.

propaganda_techniques.name: front group publication
propaganda_techniques.definition: Issuing sponsored material through a body constituted to look like an independent institute, association or patient group, whose funding relation is not disclosed.
propaganda_techniques.example: A road-freight trade body's position paper published under the name of a road-safety foundation it funds entirely.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Buys the authority of independence for material that would be discounted if correctly badged.
cues: institute names combining a virtue word with a policy domain
no funding statement, or one naming only a parent foundation
staff shared with the sponsor
output uniformly favourable to one industry
