propaganda_techniques.caution: Not every small institute is a front; the finding is the undisclosed funding relation, which has to be documented rather than inferred from the conclusion.

propaganda_techniques.name: paltering
propaganda_techniques.definition: Misleading with statements that are individually true, by selecting truths that support an inference the speaker knows to be false.
propaganda_techniques.example: Asked whether the plant had ever failed an inspection: "It has passed every inspection this year."
propaganda_techniques.effect: Produces the false belief while preserving a defence of literal accuracy, which is why it survives fact-checking and destroys trust when discovered.
cues: answers narrower than the question asked
time or scope qualifiers doing unstated work (this year, at that site)
true statements arranged to imply an untrue whole
reluctance to answer the question in its own terms
propaganda_techniques.caution: Fact-checking each sentence returns nothing; the check is whether the reader's resulting belief matches the record.

propaganda_techniques.name: pseudo-event
propaganda_techniques.definition: An occurrence staged in order to be reported — the launch, the photocall, the signing ceremony — whose only substance is the coverage it generates.
propaganda_techniques.example: A ribbon cut on a facility that has been operating for four months, arranged for the afternoon news.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Supplies the appearance of news on schedule, and displaces coverage of things that happened for reasons other than being covered.
cues: the event has no consequence other than its coverage
scheduled for a bulletin rather than for an operational reason
participants read prepared remarks and take no questions
the material fact it marks occurred earlier or not at all
propaganda_techniques.caution: Genuinely informative press conferences are pseudo-events too; the question is whether anything would have happened without the cameras, and honest coverage says so.

propaganda_techniques.name: agenda setting
propaganda_techniques.definition: Influencing not what an audience thinks but what it thinks about, by controlling which issues are made salient and how often.
propaganda_techniques.example: Four months in which every bulletin leads with the same category of crime, in a period when its incidence fell.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Salience is read by audiences as importance; an issue covered daily becomes the one against which governments are judged, independent of its size.
cues: coverage volume uncorrelated with incidence or magnitude
the same issue leading across outlets on days with no new facts
public concern rising while the underlying measure falls
propaganda_techniques.register: media analysis; for writers, a description of their own aggregate effect
propaganda_techniques.caution: Every editor sets an agenda; the neutral case becomes a fault when salience is manufactured to displace a subject the sponsor prefers unexamined.

propaganda_techniques.name: episodic framing
propaganda_techniques.definition: Presenting an issue exclusively through individual cases and incidents, with no structural context, so that audiences attribute cause and responsibility to the individuals involved.
propaganda_techniques.example: Homelessness covered as a sequence of personal biographies, with no housing supply figure in any of them.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Measurably shifts attribution from systems to persons, and therefore shifts the remedy from policy to individual reform or punishment.
cues: case after case with no aggregate figure
causes located entirely in individual choices
no policy actor named anywhere in the piece
the word 'system' absent from a system-scale problem
propaganda_techniques.caution: Episodic material is also what makes an issue readable; the fault is the exclusive diet, not the individual case. Pair the person with the base rate.

propaganda_techniques.name: thematic framing
propaganda_techniques.definition: Presenting an issue through trends, structures and aggregates, so that audiences attribute responsibility to institutions and policy.
propaganda_techniques.example: The same subject covered through twenty years of build rates, tenure change and waiting lists.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Directs attribution toward policy and away from individual culpability — the mirror of the episodic effect, and equally a choice rather than a neutral default.
cues: aggregate series with no individual case
actors named only as institutions
no scene, no person, no quotation from an affected individual
propaganda_techniques.caution: Purely thematic treatment is unreadable and lets the reader off the human cost; the honest structure alternates, and says which frame it is in.

propaganda_techniques.name: priming
propaganda_techniques.definition: Establishing, in advance of a judgement, the criteria by which the audience will make it — so that the later verdict follows from a standard set earlier by the persuader.
propaganda_techniques.example: Six weeks of coverage about competence, followed by an election in which competence is the reported issue.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Wins the argument before it is held, by fixing which of several available yardsticks is used.
cues: heavy pre-emphasis on one evaluative criterion
the criterion favours one party by construction
later coverage treats that criterion as the natural one
alternative yardsticks never mentioned
propaganda_techniques.caution: Arguing for the right standard is legitimate and should be done openly; priming is the version where the standard is installed rather than argued.

propaganda_techniques.name: threat inflation
propaganda_techniques.definition: Systematically overstating an adversary's capability or intent, usually by presenting worst-case estimates as central ones and omitting the uncertainty around them.
propaganda_techniques.example: A capability the analysts rated possible by 2035 reported as a capability the adversary has.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Justifies expenditure and emergency powers by moving the perceived distribution of outcomes, without ever making a falsifiable claim.
cues: worst-case figures quoted without their range
modal verbs dropped between the assessment and the summary (could becomes will)
capability treated as intent
no timeline attached to a projected capability
propaganda_techniques.caution: The counter is the original assessment's own language; quote the range and the modal verbs the summary removed.

propaganda_techniques.name: minimization framing
propaganda_techniques.definition: The mirror device: rendering a documented harm as smaller than the record supports, through selective units, passive construction and comparison to a worse case.
propaganda_techniques.example: A release describing forty-one deaths as an incident rate below the sector average, in the passive, with no total given.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Leaves the audience with an accurate-seeming impression of proportion that the numbers do not support, and pre-empts the demand for a response.
cues: rates given where totals are damaging
agentless passives around the harm
comparison to a worse case as the only context
diminutive vocabulary (incident, episode, isolated)
propaganda_techniques.caution: Both inflation and minimization are quantitative moves; the detection is the same in each direction — recover the unit, the denominator and the agent.

propaganda_techniques.name: personalization of the enemy
propaganda_techniques.definition: Reducing an opposing state, institution or movement to one named individual, so that the conflict is conducted as against a person rather than a structure.
propaganda_techniques.example: A trade dispute reported for a year entirely through the biography of one minister.
propaganda_techniques.effect: Simplifies mobilization and makes the conflict emotionally legible, at the cost of any account of the interests that will still exist when the person is gone.
cues: a system's actions attributed to one person's psychology
the person's name substituted for the institution throughout
removal of the individual offered as the remedy
no institutional actor named anywhere
propaganda_techniques.caution: For analysts the tell is predictive failure: personalized accounts cannot explain continuity after the individual departs.

commercial_frameworks.name: unique selling proposition
commercial_frameworks.definition: Rosser Reeves's rule that a proposition must state a specific benefit, be one the competition does not or cannot make, and be strong enough to move buyers.
commercial_frameworks.example: The only insurer that pays before the assessment, not after it.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Forces the writer to find the one contestable, checkable difference instead of restating the category's generic virtues.
commercial_frameworks.register: marketing and practical-guide register; in trade prose it survives only as a discipline for finding the real claim
commercial_frameworks.caution: Fails the house vendor test the moment it is stated in the copy's own voice — 'the only', 'uniquely positioned' — but the underlying question (what specifically is different) is worth asking of any thesis sentence.

commercial_frameworks.name: the four u's
commercial_frameworks.definition: A headline test: is it urgent, unique, ultra-specific and useful — with the working rule that three of the four are usually achievable and none is optional twice.
commercial_frameworks.example: Rewriting 'Improving your evening routine' as 'The nine-minute nightly checklist that ends the morning search for keys'.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Converts a vague title into one that names a reader, a payoff and a size, which is what makes a reader start.
commercial_frameworks.register: headline and title writing; direct-response origin
commercial_frameworks.caution: Urgency and specificity are the two most easily faked; a manufactured deadline or an invented number is the vendor-speak version, and readers of trade nonfiction discount the whole piece for it.

commercial_frameworks.name: open-loop copy
commercial_frameworks.definition: Opening a question in one sentence and answering it several sentences later, so that each unit's job is to make the next one get read.
commercial_frameworks.example: There was one line in the contract that the buyers all missed. It was not in the fine print.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Sustains attention across the passage where readers normally leave, by making stopping feel like leaving something unfinished.
commercial_frameworks.register: direct response, feature writing, popular nonfiction
commercial_frameworks.caution: A loop opened and never closed is a broken promise the reader remembers; the technique is only honest when the payoff is proportionate to the tease.

commercial_frameworks.name: the slippery slide
commercial_frameworks.definition: Joseph Sugarman's principle that every element exists to get the next one read: the headline sells the first sentence, the first sentence sells the second, and the copy is engineered so that stopping requires effort.
commercial_frameworks.example: A first sentence of four words, a second of six, neither containing a claim to argue with.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Removes every place a reader could naturally stop, which is a structural rather than a rhetorical achievement.
commercial_frameworks.caution: The technique is indifferent to the truth of what it carries, which is precisely why the reader's exit points matter; in trade nonfiction, keeping some friction is a courtesy.

commercial_frameworks.name: risk reversal
commercial_frameworks.definition: Moving the transaction's risk from the reader to the writer — the guarantee, the trial, the promise to refund without argument — stated in specific terms.
commercial_frameworks.example: Read the first two chapters; if they do not change how you file, send the book back and keep the checklist.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Removes the objection that survives every argument, which is not disbelief but unwillingness to be the one who is wrong.
commercial_frameworks.register: sales copy, offer pages; in nonfiction, the analogue is a testable promise made early
commercial_frameworks.caution: A guarantee with conditions that make it unclaimable is worse than none; readers who have tried to claim one recognize the pattern instantly.

commercial_frameworks.name: social-proof stacking
commercial_frameworks.definition: Assembling multiple independent kinds of proof — user counts, named clients, third-party awards, quoted results — so that no single item bears the weight.
commercial_frameworks.example: A number of users, two named institutions, one regulator's listing and one dated third-party test.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Different reader types accept different proofs; the stack raises the chance that each finds the one they weight.
commercial_frameworks.caution: A stack of weak proofs reads as weaker than one strong one, and this is where the vendor test bites hardest — logos in a row prove nothing and announce that nothing better was available.

commercial_frameworks.name: reason-why copy
commercial_frameworks.definition: Claude Hopkins's discipline: every claim is immediately followed by the concrete reason it is true — the process, the material, the number — rather than by an intensifier.
commercial_frameworks.example: It stays sharp because the edge is ground at seventeen degrees and the steel is through-hardened, which is unusual at this price.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Gives the reader something to check and something to repeat to someone else, which is what makes a claim travel.
commercial_frameworks.register: advertising origin; transfers directly to expository nonfiction
commercial_frameworks.caution: The move is only as good as the reason; a because-clause containing another adjective is the vendor-speak failure and is easy to miss in one's own draft.

commercial_frameworks.name: the long-copy principle
commercial_frameworks.definition: The direct-response finding that length is not the enemy of response — interested readers read on, and each additional true, relevant fact removes an objection.
commercial_frameworks.example: A four-thousand-word letter that outsells a four-hundred-word one because it answers the six questions the short version left standing.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Reframes cutting as a question of relevance rather than of word count: cut what does not answer an objection, keep what does however long the result.
commercial_frameworks.register: direct response; the principle transfers to any writing with a persuasive burden
commercial_frameworks.caution: The finding is about interested readers; length applied to an audience that has not yet been given a reason to care simply exposes more places to stop.

commercial_frameworks.name: the p.s. line
commercial_frameworks.definition: A closing postscript that restates the single most important point, on the direct-mail finding that the postscript is among the most-read elements of a letter.
commercial_frameworks.example: P.S. The rate changes on the thirty-first. Nothing else in this letter has a deadline.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Catches the reader who scanned, and gives the writer one more chance to state the whole ask in one sentence.
commercial_frameworks.caution: In trade prose the equivalent is the last line of a chapter, not a literal postscript; a real P.S. in a book reads as sales material and fails the vendor test outright.

commercial_frameworks.name: bucket brigade
commercial_frameworks.definition: Short transitional phrases dropped between passages — here is the part that matters, but there is a catch — that carry the reader over a natural stopping point.
commercial_frameworks.example: So far, so ordinary. Then the second invoice arrived.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Rebuilds momentum at the paragraph seam, which is where scanning readers leave.
commercial_frameworks.register: online writing, direct response, popular nonfiction
commercial_frameworks.caution: The device is heavily marked; three in a chapter is a voice, six is a content mill, and in a book the transition families do the same work without the smell.

commercial_frameworks.name: the big-idea lead
commercial_frameworks.definition: Opening on one large, previously unstated idea that reorganizes what the reader already knows, rather than on the offer, the problem or the story.
commercial_frameworks.example: Every argument about the shortage assumes the register is complete. It has not been complete since 1994.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Buys the reader's whole attention at once, and makes the rest of the piece the working out of a proposition they now want settled.
commercial_frameworks.register: sales letters, feature openings, book proposals
commercial_frameworks.caution: A big idea that the body cannot deliver is the most damaging opening available; the reader's disappointment is proportionate to the promise.

commercial_frameworks.name: the rule of one
commercial_frameworks.definition: The copywriting constraint that a piece addresses one reader, carries one big idea, makes one promise and asks for one action.
commercial_frameworks.example: A chapter that could have covered three reforms and covers the one the reader can act on this year.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Prevents the dilution that occurs when a text tries to serve every segment, and produces something a reader can restate afterwards.
commercial_frameworks.register: direct response; a useful discipline for chapter and section planning
commercial_frameworks.caution: Applied to a genuinely multi-part argument it forces false simplification; the rule governs the ask, not the analysis.

commercial_frameworks.name: objection handling block
commercial_frameworks.definition: A passage that voices the reader's likely objections in their own words and answers each, placed where the objection actually occurs to them.
commercial_frameworks.example: You are thinking that this only works for large authorities. It also works for the smallest, and here is the parish that did it.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Converts silent resistance into an exchange the writer can win, and demonstrates that the objection was anticipated rather than missed.
commercial_frameworks.caution: Voicing an objection weaker than the reader's real one is the copywriting cousin of the straw man and is transparent to anyone holding the strong version.

commercial_frameworks.name: value stacking
commercial_frameworks.definition: Enumerating the components of an offer with a value assigned to each, so that the total accumulates before the price is named.
commercial_frameworks.example: The template, the annual update, the two hours of support, each priced, then the single figure for all three.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Sets a reference point against which the price is judged, and converts a single decision into an arithmetic one.
commercial_frameworks.caution: The device is the purest vendor-speak in the category and the component values are usually fictitious; it appears here so writers can recognize it in sources they quote.

commercial_frameworks.name: the specificity premium
commercial_frameworks.definition: The direct-response finding that exact figures outpull round ones, because precision reads as measurement and roundness reads as estimate.
commercial_frameworks.example: Not 'about half of applications' but 'four hundred and eleven of eight hundred and nine'.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Raises belief at no cost when the number is real, and gives the reader something they can carry into an argument with someone else.
commercial_frameworks.caution: Precision beyond what the method supports is spurious precision, and a reader who catches one false decimal place discounts every other figure in the piece.

commercial_frameworks.name: the damaging admission
commercial_frameworks.definition: Naming a real drawback of the thing being argued for, early and without softening, before the case for it.
commercial_frameworks.example: It is slower than what you use now, it costs more per unit, and it is the only method that survives an audit.
commercial_frameworks.effect: The admitted flaw certifies the rest; a reader who has seen one true negative extends provisional credit to the positives.
commercial_frameworks.register: direct response, honest sales writing, argumentative nonfiction
commercial_frameworks.caution: Admitting a flaw nobody minds is the standard fake — it performs candour while conceding nothing, and experienced readers grade it as vendor-speak.

commercial_frameworks.name: the deadline close
commercial_frameworks.definition: Ending on a genuine, dated limit — a closing consultation, a price change, a finite stock — that converts intention into action.
commercial_frameworks.example: Objections close on the eleventh; after that the classification stands for ten years.
commercial_frameworks.effect: Defeats the reader's default, which is not refusal but postponement.
commercial_frameworks.caution: The manufactured version — a countdown that resets, a limit that never binds — is the most reputation-destroying move in commercial writing, and it is the one readers check.

narrative_persuasion.name: narrative transportation
narrative_persuasion.definition: The mechanism by which absorption in a story reduces a reader's resistance: attention, imagery and feeling are committed to the narrative world and are not available for counterarguing.
narrative_persuasion.example: Twelve pages inside a shift at the depot, after which the reader accepts a claim about scheduling they would have contested as a proposition.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Belief change that persists after the story's details are forgotten, and that the reader experiences as their own conclusion.
narrative_persuasion.register: narrative nonfiction, fiction with an argument, health and advocacy communication
narrative_persuasion.caution: The mechanism is indifferent to accuracy — a false story transports as well as a true one — which is why transported readers should be given the checkable material afterwards.

narrative_persuasion.name: burkean identification
narrative_persuasion.definition: Kenneth Burke's account of persuasion as consubstantiality: the writer establishes shared substance — interests, experience, vocabulary — so that the audience's assent follows from being addressed as the same kind of person.
narrative_persuasion.example: An argument to farmers written from inside the problem of a harvest window rather than about it.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Assent that does not feel like being persuaded, because the reader is agreeing with someone they recognize as one of themselves.
narrative_persuasion.caution: Identification claimed without substance is the plain-folks device; the difference is whether the shared substance is real and would survive scrutiny.

narrative_persuasion.name: the trojan-horse anecdote
narrative_persuasion.definition: A story admitted for its human interest that carries the argument's premise inside it, so the premise is accepted as part of the story rather than assessed as a claim.
narrative_persuasion.example: The account of one clerk's morning contains, unremarked, the fact that the two systems cannot see each other — which is the chapter's whole case.
narrative_persuasion.effect: The load-bearing premise enters below the level at which readers argue, and is available as agreed ground later.
narrative_persuasion.caution: The move is legitimate when the smuggled premise is true and independently evidenced elsewhere; used to install a contested claim it is manipulation with a narrative wrapper.

narrative_persuasion.name: exemplification effect
narrative_persuasion.definition: Zillmann's finding that vivid individual exemplars dominate base-rate information in audience judgement, even when the base rate is stated in the same text.
narrative_persuasion.example: A piece giving the correct one-in-forty-thousand risk alongside two interviews with affected families, after which readers estimate the risk far higher.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Determines what the audience takes away regardless of what the text states; the case beats the number in memory and in subsequent judgement.
narrative_persuasion.caution: Knowing this is a duty as well as a tool: a writer who pairs an unrepresentative case with an accurate base rate has still, predictably, misinformed the reader.

narrative_persuasion.name: the conversion narrative
narrative_persuasion.definition: As a persuasive structure: the writer recounts having held the reader's current position, the specific evidence that dislodged it, and what changed afterwards.
narrative_persuasion.example: I ran the programme for six years and defended it in print twice. The audit is what changed my mind, and here is the page.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Models the change being asked for and pre-empts the reader's sense that the writer never understood the other side — the reader is being asked to make a journey the writer has already made.
narrative_persuasion.caution: A conversion the reader suspects was never real is the most alienating thing in persuasive nonfiction; the former position has to be stated at its strongest and dated.

narrative_persuasion.name: testimony structure
narrative_persuasion.definition: The witness's own account given its own shape — what I saw, where I stood, what I could not see — with the writer's framing minimized to establishing the standing to speak.
narrative_persuasion.example: Three pages in one voice, and one sentence beforehand saying where she was standing and for how long.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Carries the authority of first-hand knowledge and its limits at the same time, which paraphrase destroys in both directions.
narrative_persuasion.register: oral history, human-rights reporting, documentary nonfiction
narrative_persuasion.caution: Testimony is evidence with known failure modes; presenting it as unmediated truth rather than as one witness's account is where the form's persuasive force outruns its warrant.

narrative_persuasion.name: parable deployment
narrative_persuasion.definition: Telling a short, self-contained story whose application is left to the reader, and then proceeding as though it had been made.
narrative_persuasion.example: The story of the two harbours, told in a paragraph, followed by a return to the regulator without a stated moral.
narrative_persuasion.effect: The reader performs the mapping onto the argument themselves, which produces a firmer commitment than a stated analogy.
narrative_persuasion.caution: A parable whose mapping is ambiguous will be mapped wrongly and cannot be corrected without destroying the device; test it on a reader before relying on it.

narrative_persuasion.name: reader-as-protagonist frame
narrative_persuasion.definition: Structuring the piece so the reader occupies the deciding role — the information arrives as it would to them, and the choice is presented as theirs before the outcome is revealed.
narrative_persuasion.example: You have the two reports, the budget and eleven days. The chapter then describes what the committee actually did.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Produces sympathy for a decision the reader would otherwise judge, and makes the eventual verdict theirs to revise rather than the writer's to impose.
narrative_persuasion.register: narrative nonfiction, case-based teaching, decision writing
narrative_persuasion.caution: Only honest if the reader is given the information the decider actually had; loading the frame with hindsight makes the exercise a trap and readers resent it.

narrative_persuasion.name: entertainment-education
narrative_persuasion.definition: Embedding a factual or behavioural message inside a story designed primarily to be enjoyed, on the Sabido model — a serial narrative with positive, negative and transitional characters.
narrative_persuasion.example: A radio serial in which the transitional character's decision about the clinic is the season's emotional payoff.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Reaches audiences no informational campaign reaches, and does its work through identification with the transitional character rather than through instruction.
narrative_persuasion.register: broadcast drama, public health communication, some children's nonfiction
narrative_persuasion.caution: The form is paternalistic by construction; the ethical version discloses its sponsorship and gets the underlying facts right, because the audience cannot separate the message from the story afterwards.

narrative_persuasion.name: counterarguing suppression
narrative_persuasion.definition: The measured drop in a reader's production of counterarguments while absorbed in narrative, and the writer's decision whether to exploit or offset it.
narrative_persuasion.example: A chapter that gives the story first and then, deliberately, three paragraphs of the strongest objection while the reader is still inside it.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Determines whether narrative persuasion produces a belief that survives the reader meeting the counter-case, or one that collapses at the first encounter.
narrative_persuasion.caution: Beliefs installed under suppressed counterarguing are unstable and their collapse takes the writer's credibility with them; offsetting is self-interested as well as honest.

narrative_persuasion.name: the counter-story
narrative_persuasion.definition: A narrative told deliberately against a dominant one, from the position the dominant account leaves out, whose persuasive claim is that the accepted story is itself a story.
narrative_persuasion.example: The same road scheme narrated from the four households whose access it removed, against thirty years of accounts written from the traffic model.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Denaturalizes the received version by demonstrating that it had a viewpoint, which no direct refutation of it achieves.
narrative_persuasion.caution: A counter-story is an argument and carries the same burdens; positioned as beyond challenge because of whose story it is, it forfeits the standing it was making a case for.

narrative_persuasion.name: narrative paradigm test
narrative_persuasion.definition: Walter Fisher's two criteria by which audiences actually judge stories: coherence, whether it hangs together, and fidelity, whether it rings true against what the listener knows of how life goes.
narrative_persuasion.example: An account that survives every documentary check and is disbelieved because nobody in it behaves the way people behave.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Explains why evidentially strong accounts fail and evidentially weak ones persuade, and gives the writer two auditable questions to ask of a draft.
narrative_persuasion.caution: Fidelity is a measure of conformity to the audience's existing beliefs, not of truth; a true account of an unusual event will fail the test and needs evidential support to compensate.

narrative_persuasion.name: protagonist selection
narrative_persuasion.definition: Choosing whose story carries the argument, from among the many people the situation contains.
narrative_persuasion.example: The chapter could follow the campaigner, the officer or the family; it follows the officer, and the argument changes accordingly.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Determines the reader's default sympathies and what counts as the problem, before any claim is made.
narrative_persuasion.caution: Selecting only the most sympathetic subject — the perfect victim — makes the argument depend on the subject's blamelessness and concedes that less perfect cases deserve less.

narrative_persuasion.name: drama triangle framing
narrative_persuasion.definition: Casting a situation into the three roles of victim, persecutor and rescuer, which audiences fill in automatically once any one role is occupied.
narrative_persuasion.example: A regulatory dispute narrated so that the agency is the rescuer, and every subsequent fact is read for which role it supports.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Instantly legible and strongly persuasive, because the reader knows the shape and can predict where sympathy goes.
narrative_persuasion.caution: Most institutional situations have no such roles, and forcing them produces an account that cannot survive contact with the participants; the rescuer role in particular tends to be the writer's own.

narrative_persuasion.name: heroic framing
narrative_persuasion.definition: Narrating a complex, distributed achievement or failure as one person's journey against obstacles, because that shape is the most transmissible one available.
narrative_persuasion.example: A twelve-year collaboration between four laboratories told as the story of the researcher who gave the conference talk.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Enormously memorable and quotable, and a systematic misdescription of how the thing happened.
narrative_persuasion.register: popular science, business writing, profile journalism
narrative_persuasion.caution: The cost is paid by the reader's model of how such things work — heroic accounts teach that the solution is a person, which makes the next attempt at the same problem worse.

narrative_persuasion.name: the just-so story
narrative_persuasion.definition: An explanatory narrative constructed backwards from a known outcome, whose coherence is mistaken by the reader — and often by the writer — for evidence of the mechanism it describes.
narrative_persuasion.example: Every step of a firm's collapse presented as inevitable, in an account written after the collapse and unable to explain the four competitors that did the same things and survived.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Produces confident understanding of a process the account has not actually established, and is highly resistant to correction because it explains everything.
narrative_persuasion.register: business history, popular evolutionary and economic writing
narrative_persuasion.caution: The test is whether the same narrative would have been written about the counterfactual outcome; if it would, it explains nothing.

narrative_persuasion.name: the composite protagonist
narrative_persuasion.definition: A single narrated person assembled from several real ones, used to carry a pattern that no individual case demonstrates cleanly.
narrative_persuasion.example: A named caseworker whose day contains events from four different caseworkers' months.
narrative_persuasion.effect: Achieves narrative economy and typicality at the cost of the reader's warranted belief that they are reading about a person who exists.
narrative_persuasion.register: nonfiction where it is disclosed, and a serious breach where it is not
narrative_persuasion.caution: In reported nonfiction the composite is a fabrication unless flagged at the point of use — a note at the back is not disclosure — and its discovery ends the book's evidential standing.

narrative_persuasion.name: the unstated moral
narrative_persuasion.definition: Ending the narrative at its last concrete fact and declining to state the lesson the whole piece was arranged to produce.
narrative_persuasion.example: The chapter ends with the register still open on the counter, and does not say what that means.
narrative_persuasion.effect: The reader states the moral to themselves, which is the version they will repeat to other people.
narrative_persuasion.caution: Only works when a single reading is available; where the material genuinely supports two morals, withholding is not restraint but evasion, and readers take the easier one.
